newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE - New systems, partners to spur Taiwan bond market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New systems, partners to spur Taiwan bond market.

text.p: Taiwan's new quoting and trading system and planned establishment of the island's first credit rating agency will improve efficiency and sharply boost turnover in an already robust bond market, experts and officials say.
The innovations are seen having their most significant effect on Taiwan's corporate debt market, as firms frustrated by the stock market's vagaries look for alternative financing.

In July, the watchdog Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) helped the bond market establish a nationwide yield-to-maturity matching system that in just two months has been put into use by 26 major bond-trading securities brokerages.

"Since these 26 brokerages account for some 80 percent of Taiwan's bond trading turnover, the system offers nationwide transparency in dealing information and convenience in trading," Lin Ying-che, the SEC's bond chief, told Reuters.

"With the new matching system, Taiwan's bond market trading turnover is expected to grow much further in coming years, with this year's growth of some 30 percent over 1995," said Lin, the agency's deputy director in charge of bond trading.
Taiwan's bond market turnover first overtook stock market turnover in 1992 and has never looked back.
In 1995, central bank figures show bond market turnover was T$20.8 trillion (US$756 billion) -- more than double the stock market's T$10.15 trillion (US$369 billion).
What's more, SEC figures show average monthly bond turnover surging to T$2.21 trillion (US$80 billion) in the first seven months of 1996, 27 percent higher than the 1995 monthly average.
Analysts praised the SEC's matching-system nudge.
"It's a big step forward for market development, helping Taiwan toward a more mature bond market," said Eric Chien, assistant vice-president at Union Bank of Switzerland Taiwan.
"From now on, we can have a standardised screen price to follow, a very important signal in the market," Chien said.
MATCHING SYSTEM MAY NEED FURTHER IMPROVEMENT
A manager at another foreign firm, who asked not to be named, cautioned that the matching system needs further improvement.

"Many securities brokerages still complain about the system as they still encounter problems in delivery and settlement in bond trading," she said. "Some have suggested that a central clearing house is needed for the system."
In August, the SEC said it would seek a foreign partner to help form Taiwan's first credit-rating agency in its drive to become an Asia-Pacific financial centre.
The foreign partner would hold less than half of the new venture, whose mimimum paid-in capital would be T$200 million (US$7.3 million), the SEC said.
Standard & Poor's Corp is among firms it has contacted.
"We plan to set up a preparatory office for the new credit trading agency in September, and hope it can start operations in January 1997," said a Commission official.
The agency will rate credit on bonds, commercial paper and financial institutions, offering reference for investors and related financial institutions.
NEW CREDIT RATING AGENCY WILL HELP LOCAL FIRMS WITH BONDS
"The new credit rating agency will help local firms issue corporate bonds," said SEC bond chief Lin. "It will help local firms to issue bonds overseas and help foreign firms to issue bonds here."
Government bonds dominate Taiwan's bond-trading pie.
Corporate bond trading was only T$4.69 billion (US$171 million) in 1995, or 0.023 percent of total 1995 bond market turnover, according to the central bank.
But in May 1996, corporate bond trading began to surge.
In June alone, corporate bond turnover reached T$7.69 billion (US$280 million) -- or 0.3 percent of the total market turnover of T$2.42 trillion (US$88 billion).
"Local companies, seeing how hard it is to raise funds in the stock market now, are issuing more corporate bonds, thus expanding corporate bond trading," Lin said.
Expecting interest rates to fall, many Taiwan firms have issued more corporate bonds because financing bond issues is much cheaper than borrowing from a bank, analysts said.
Beneficial tax changes also are expected.
"Parliament appears to be inclined to pass a proposal to scrap the securities transaction tax on corporate bonds, now at 0.1 percent," Lin said.
Taiwan does not collect a securities transaction tax on government bonds.
Government bond issuance first surged in 1991 when spending for the state's Six-Year National Development led to large deficits and a need for large amounts of debt financing.

As of June 1996, outstanding central government bond issues totalled T$786 billion (US$29 billion), compared with T$33.3 billion (US$1.2 billion) by the provincial government and T$18.3 billion (US$665 million) by city governments.
Outstanding corporate bonds of private firms totalled just T$130.9 billion (US$4.76 billion), and those of state-run firms T$25.7 billion (US$935 million).

Private firms issued T$15.59 billion (US$567 million) and T$28.7 billion (US$1.04 billion) worth of corporate bonds in May and June 1996, respectively -- more than the T$38.79 billion (US$1.41 billion) in the whole of 1995.
The SEC allows foreign firms to issue bonds in Taiwan but none has done so.

Only one international institution, the Asian Development Bank, has issued bonds on Taiwan. In August 1995, the ADB issued a seven-year Taiwan dollar-denominated bond valued at T$2.6 billion (US$95 million). It plans to issue US$200 million Taiwan dollar-denominated bonds in October, the central bank has said.
The ADB issues are seen as helping to internationalise Taiwan's bond market and raising the credibility of Taiwan's currency.
To further develop the bond market, the central bank has said it plans to introduce book entry system to limit risk.
"The book entry system, if enforced, can help reduce delivery risks," Chien said.
But he said the local market lacks a short-selling system to help stabilise bond prices.
Taiwan is scheduled to set up its own futures market in early 1997, and the SEC said it plans to set up interest rate futures related to bond trading.
(Conversion US$1 = T$27.5)
